newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists say Tiananmen commemorations banned.
newsitem.headline: HK activists say Tiananmen commemorations banned.

text.p: Hong Kong pro-democracy activists accused authorities on Saturday of restricting freedom of expression by refusing permission for memorials to the victims of the Tiananmen massacre in 1989.

The Hong Alliance in Support of Democratic Movements in China said authorities turned down three applications to display sculpture symbolising the fight for freedom in parks next week to mark the eighth anniversary of the bloodshed on June 4.
"It is clear they are using political criteria to object to the Hong Kong Alliance's activities," Alliance Vice Chairman Mak Hoi-wah said.
The association expects tens of thousands of people to rally this year in the last set of memorial marches and vigils before the British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
"In China...they can use the whole Tiananmen Square on June 4 for official use and don't allow the people to go there and mourn (the victims of) the June 4 massacre," he said.
"This kind of activity will be going on here. They will...not allow the Hong Kong Alliance to organise its normal activities as we have done in past years," Mak said.
Almost one million Hong Kong people poured onto the streets in 1989 in protest against the killings of democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa has said he will not ban commemoration events but told pro-democracy activists this week to forget the mourning and look to the future.

Public concern is rising that Hong Kong's cherished freedoms may be curtailed after the handover following Tung's decision to implement Chinese plans to roll back civil liberties laws and scrap the British-style electoral system.
Tung's amendments include a ban on foreign political funding and new limits on the right to protest and freedom of association. New electoral laws have yet to be drafted.
Tung's office is working on a set of guidelines for the police to implement the new laws, aide Fanny Law told reporters on Saturday.
She said the guidelines will cover the definition of "national security", which critics have said the definition of national security is vague and can be abused.

"(For example), if a society is formed with the sole purpose of promoting the independence of Taiwan, then we would not, definitely not, allow this because this would be threatening to the territorial integrity of China," Law said.
China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and objects firmly to its independence.
